beats.intro: Chapter nine, lesson five. Pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle. [[round]]Picture a roundabout. Cars drive in, circle once, and drive out. The roundabout itself never wears out, and it is ready for the next car. [[map]]Here is our map of cellular respiration. Glycolysis is done, and it left us with pyruvate. [[lit]]Today we light up the next two parts, inside the mitochondrion: pyruvate oxidation, and a roundabout of chemistry called the citric acid cycle.
beats.enter: [[mito]]With oxygen present, pyruvate leaves the cytosol and enters the mitochondrion, through a transport protein. [[pyr]]Remember what it is: a chain of three carbons. Before the cycle can begin, pyruvate must be converted to acetyl co-A, which links the cycle to glycolysis. The enzyme is pyruvate dehydrogenase, a big complex of many subunits, and it works in three steps. [[co2]]Step one. The carboxyl carbon, one of the three, is cut off and leaves as carbon dioxide. [[nadh]]Step two. The two carbons that remain are oxidized. Their electrons go to N A D plus, which becomes N A D H. [[coa]]Step three. Coenzyme A, a carrier molecule, attaches to what is left. [[acetyl]]That is acetyl co-A: two carbons, the acetyl group, riding on coenzyme A. [[count]]Count the carbons. Three went in. One left as carbon dioxide, and two carry on. Some books call this the link reaction, because it links glycolysis to the cycle.
beats.q1: Quick check. What happens to pyruvate in pyruvate oxidation?
beats.cycle: [[wheel]]Now the citric acid cycle, also called the Krebs cycle. It takes place in the mitochondrial matrix. Here the fuel derived from pyruvate is oxidized completely, and the cycle has eight steps, each run by its own specific enzyme. [[join]]In step one, the two carbon acetyl group joins oxaloacetate, a four carbon molecule. Two plus four makes six: the product is citrate, the six carbon molecule that gives the cycle its name. Coenzyme A is released, free to pick up another acetyl group. [[loop]]The next seven steps rearrange and oxidize the molecule, step by step, until it becomes oxaloacetate again. That is why it is a cycle. The roundabout comes back to its starting point, and oxaloacetate is ready for the next acetyl group.
beats.steps: [[s2]]Let's walk around it once. In step two, citrate is rearranged into its isomer, isocitrate. [[s3]]In step three, isocitrate is oxidized, and N A D plus becomes N A D H. Then it loses a carbon dioxide. The molecule now has five carbons. [[s4]]In step four, another carbon dioxide leaves, and again N A D plus becomes N A D H. What remains is attached to coenzyme A, by a high energy bond, as succinyl co-A. Four carbons are left. [[s5]]In step five, that high energy bond pays for something. A phosphate group is passed to G D P, making G T P, and G T P can hand it on to make A T P. [[s6]]In step six, two hydrogens go to a different carrier, called F A D, making F A D H two. [[s7]]In step seven, water is added, and the bonds rearrange. [[s8]]In step eight, the molecule is oxidized, N A D plus becomes N A D H once more, and out comes oxaloacetate. You do not need to memorize the names. Just notice the pattern: carbon dioxide leaves twice, electrons are collected again and again, and one A T P is made.
beats.turn: [[tally]]So one turn of the cycle makes one A T P, three N A D H, and one F A D H two. And two carbon dioxide have left. [[carriers]]The N A D H and F A D H two now hold the electrons taken from the food. They relay them to the electron transport chain, which is where most of the energy will be harvested.
beats.q2: Quick check. How many N A D H does one turn of the cycle make?
beats.carbons: Now a carbon audit. This part is our own arithmetic, built from the slides. [[glc]]One glucose has six carbons. [[two]]Glycolysis makes two pyruvate, three carbons each. So everything from here happens twice. [[po]]Each pyruvate gives one carbon dioxide in pyruvate oxidation, and an acetyl group of two carbons. Two pyruvate, two carbon dioxide. [[cyc]]Each acetyl group enters the cycle, and the cycle sends out two carbon dioxide per turn. Two turns, four carbon dioxide. [[six]]Two plus four is six carbon dioxide. All six carbons of glucose have left as carbon dioxide, which is exactly what you breathe out.
beats.glucose: [[tot]]And the totals per glucose, also our own sums. Pyruvate oxidation gives two N A D H. Two turns of the cycle give six N A D H, two F A D H two, and two A T P. [[so]]Notice something. Glycolysis and the cycle together made only four A T P directly. [[carr]]But look at all those carriers: eight N A D H and two F A D H two from this stage, plus the two N A D H from glycolysis, all full of electrons. That is where the energy is waiting. The next lessons show how it becomes A T P. [[o2]]And notice that oxygen has not been used up in any step so far. It waits at the end of the chain.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]With oxygen, pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is oxidized to acetyl co-A, losing one carbon dioxide and making one N A D H. [[s2]]In the matrix, the acetyl group joins oxaloacetate to make citrate, and eight steps later oxaloacetate is back. [[s3]]Each turn makes one A T P, three N A D H and one F A D H two, and gives off two carbon dioxide. [[s4]]Two turns per glucose, and all six carbons are gone. [[end]]Now try the practice.
